Michelin Street Food
intro: This is the street food Michelin inspectors queued up for themselves: 14 Bib Gourmand spots, from pushcarts to charcoal grills at the curb. Start with K. Panich, whose mango sticky rice follows a recipe handed down from the royal kitchens of Rama V and VI. Then Phuket's Pathongko Mae Pranee, where the second generation stuffs its fritters with crab and cheese, and Somsak Pu Ob, serving clay-pot crab and glass noodles fresh off the fire.
quickAnswerHtml: A lineup of 14 Bib Gourmand street food spots from the 2026 Michelin Guide Thailand, led by K. Panich and its royal-recipe mango sticky rice.

blocks.html: This is the street food Michelin inspectors queued up for themselves: 14 Bib Gourmand spots, from pushcarts to charcoal grills at the curb. Start with K. Panich, whose mango sticky rice follows a recipe handed down from the royal kitchens of Rama V and VI. Then Phuket's Pathongko Mae Pranee, where the second generation stuffs its fritters with crab and cheese, and Somsak Pu Ob, serving clay-pot crab and glass noodles fresh off the fire.

blocks.name: A Pong Mae Sunee
blocks.descHtml:
A Pong Mae Sunee is a street-side stall on Soi Sun Uthit, near Yaowarat Road, right in the middle of Phuket Old Town — an easy walk from Thalang Road and the Sino-Portuguese shophouse district. Open every day from 09:00 to around 14:00 (MICHELIN lists 14:00; Wongnai lists as late as 16:00), but the real thing to know is that it usually sells out before closing, since everything is made one piece at a time over charcoal and buyers never stop coming. Go in the late morning before noon for the best shot, and if you want to check ahead, call 086-743-7557.

Each piece is just 5–6 THB, so 20–50 THB is plenty to eat well. No booking needed at all — it's walk-in only, and cash only, so bring small bills or coins. While you're in line, it's worth just watching the tiny pans spin over the charcoal. The trick is to order and eat right there while it's still hot, when the edges are at their crispiest. It makes a great first stop on a morning walking the old town, before moving on to cafes and local restaurants in the same neighborhood. Read the full review →
blocks.signature: A pong — an old-school coconut crepe grilled one piece at a time over charcoal, crisp edges, soft center, 5–6 THB a piece
mustOrder: A pong (old-school coconut crepe, crisp edges, soft coconut-scented center, best eaten hot off the pan)
blocks.bestFor: Anyone walking Phuket Old Town who wants a taste of local sweets for pocket change, Bib Gourmand level
blocks.libCredit: Photo: Khanom A Pong Mae Sunee Phuket official Facebook page

blocks.name: Bunloet (Pom Prap Sattru Phai)
blocks.descHtml:
Easy on the wallet — 40-95 baht a dish, egg-noodle-with-grilled-pork bowls at 60-80 baht, stewed chicken wings at 80 baht, eating your fill costs under 100 baht per head. The restaurant is walk-in only with no booking system, though you can call ahead to ask or pre-order at 06-2624-9269. Seating is about 40 spots, with an air-conditioned section (an extra 5 baht per head), cash only, and delivery available through the apps if you'd rather not make the trip.

Timing your visit is the most important part. The restaurant is open daily during the day, roughly 09:00/10:00-17:00, and once they sell out, that's it — go before 3pm if you can, especially if you're set on the charcoal-grilled soy-sauce pork, which is cooked in batches and, once gone, means waiting or missing out. As for getting there, the restaurant is at 360, at the mouth of Nakhon Sawan 8 alley, Nakhon Sawan Road, Pom Prap Sattru Phai district, in the Nang Loeng market–Wat Sommanat area — there's no train station within walking distance, so the closest option is connecting from MRT Sam Yot or Hua Lamphong; a taxi or motorbike taxi the rest of the way is the easier bet. Read the full review →

blocks.signature: Egg-noodle-with-grilled-pork — pork shoulder marinated in soy sauce, sugar, and pepper, grilled over charcoal in batches
mustOrder: Egg-noodle-with-grilled-pork (signature dish, soy-sauce-marinated pork shoulder grilled over charcoal)
Red pork and crispy pork over rice
blocks.bestFor: Egg-noodle lovers and Bib Gourmand fans on a sub-100-baht budget who want real charcoal-grilled soy-sauce pork in the old Nang Loeng neighbourhood

blocks.name: Jok Guay Jab Tom Sen Bat Queue
blocks.descHtml:
The restaurant sits at the entrance to Bang Lam Phu Market on Thanon Na Mueang, right in the center of Khon Kaen, open daily from evening to late night, roughly 17:00–01:30 (some sources say it opens as early as 15:00). Bowls run 35–80 THB, easy on the wallet. No reservations — just walk in — but during the busy evening stretch, around 7–9pm, it gets packed and you'll need to grab a queue ticket before ordering, which is where the restaurant's name comes from. The MICHELIN tip: if you're short on time, eat in rather than queuing for takeaway — it's faster.

Worth ordering: Vietnamese-style guay jab with moo yor, tom sen with chicken feet, pork jok with a soft-boiled egg added, and kao lao pork-neck-bone soup. For takeaway or delivery, call 086-646-5056 or 043-320-207. Getting there is easy since Bang Lam Phu Market is a landmark known across all of Khon Kaen, within walking distance of the Khon Kaen City Pillar Shrine. Best times to go: arrive before 6pm to skip the wait, or come late after 10pm for a last meal of the night. There are smaller branches behind Khon Kaen University and at Ton Tan Market, but the branch that holds the MICHELIN distinction is this one on Thanon Na Mueang. Read the full review →
blocks.cuisine: Street food · Jok, Vietnamese guay jab, tom sen
blocks.signature: Vietnamese-style guay jab with pork rib, moo yor, and a soft-boiled egg, as recommended by the MICHELIN inspector
mustOrder: Vietnamese-style guay jab with moo yor
blocks.bestFor: Cheap dinner-to-late-night eats in central Khon Kaen for street food fans who want a real roadside Bib Gourmand restaurant
blocks.foodType: Street food · Jok, Vietnamese guay jab, tom sen

blocks.name: K. Panich
blocks.descHtml:
The budget to prepare is light. Mango sticky rice runs about THB 130 a box (around THB 160 for delivery), while plain coconut sticky rice for pairing at home costs about THB 240 a kilogram. The thing people miss most often: the shop takes cash only, so bring notes before you queue. No bookings are taken since it's a pure takeaway shop — if you want to check stock before leaving your hotel, call 02-221-3554 or 062-740-3553, and it's also available through LINE MAN for lazy days.

The shop is open Monday to Saturday roughly 07:00-18:00 (MICHELIN lists closing at 17:00, so build in a buffer to be safe), and during mango season from January to June it opens every day with no closed days. The best time to go is early morning right when it opens at seven, because during peak mango season especially March to June the queue runs long from late morning into the afternoon, and mangoes often sell out before evening. Go early and every topping is available with no gamble. Getting there: take the MRT to Sam Yot station, then walk about 10 minutes to Tanao Road, near Sao Ching Cha — it pairs perfectly with a walking route around Rattanakosin Island. Read the full review →
blocks.area: Sao Ching Cha / Phra Nakhon (Rattanakosin Island)
blocks.signature: Mango sticky rice with a recipe passed down from the royal kitchens of Rama V-VI, steamed with Chumphon coconut and Khiao Ngu sticky rice from Chiang Rai
mustOrder: Sticky rice with egg custard topping
Plain coconut sticky rice (bought by the kilogram)
blocks.bestFor: Dessert lovers and anyone planning a walk around Rattanakosin Island who wants to carry home royal-kitchen-style mango sticky rice
blocks.hours: Mon-Sat ~07:00-18:00; during mango season (Jan-Jun) open daily /

blocks.name: Khanom Ochin
blocks.descHtml:
Khanom Ochin is a takeaway-only cart with no seating, on Chomsurangyat Road near the Nong Bua Rong intersection, in Korat's old town, not far from the Thao Suranari Monument, which doubles as a handy landmark for finding it. It's very easy on the wallet — under THB 100 a head — cash only, no advance booking. You'll need to queue in person (walk-in only). There's a phone number, 062-684-2484, for questions.

The cart starts selling around 3pm (MICHELIN lists 15:00-21:00), but in practice it sells out well before closing time, and usually earlier than the official hours suggest. The queue is legendary — people start lining up before 3pm — so the best time to go is right at opening, or a little before. Don't come in the evening; you'll likely find nothing left. One key thing to remember: the cart is closed on Wednesdays and Sundays, so plan your trip accordingly before driving out. The must-order is the salty Khanom Ochin — crispy fried dough wrapped around boldly seasoned glass noodles and vegetables — plus the homemade fried steamed buns. Grab extra to take home for family so you don't regret it later. Read the full review →
blocks.signature: Salty Khanom Ochin — crispy fried dough wrapped around boldly seasoned glass-noodle-and-vegetable filling, a name only used in Korat and found nowhere else in Thailand
mustOrder: Salty Khanom Ochin (crispy fried dough with glass noodles and vegetables)
blocks.bestFor: Street food fans who want to bag a MICHELIN spot for under THB 100, and anyone passing through Korat looking for a one-of-a-kind souvenir snack

blocks.name: Khao Lam Mae Khai Toon Klao
blocks.descHtml:
Khao Lam Mae Khai Toon Klao is at 357 Sukhumvit Road, Saen Suk sub-district, Nong Mon area, Chon Buri, right across from the PTT petrol station in Nong Mon. Driving from Bangkok via the motorway toward Bang Saen, you'll pass right by the shop. It's open roughly 08:00-17:00 or until sold out, and closed every Wednesday — don't forget to check the day before you go. This is a takeaway-only shop with no seating, cash only, no advance booking needed, but if you want to order a large quantity or check whether stock remains, call 086-512-8498 or 081-453-0405

Sold by the tube, a budget under THB 200 per person gets you several tubes to take home. Both white and black sticky rice are available, in long and short tubes. Taro and black bean fillings are available every day, while custard filling is made only on Saturdays and Sundays. The best time to go is in the morning, since the shop grills khao lam fresh daily over charcoal and it sells out fast, especially on holidays when plenty of people stop by on their way to Bang Saen. Arrive in the late afternoon and you risk coming away empty-handed. Pair the trip with Bang Saen beach, just a few minutes further down the road Read the full review →
blocks.signature: Fresh coconut milk khao lam grilled over charcoal, fragrant with bamboo, filled with taro, black bean, and custard
mustOrder: White/black sticky rice khao lam (long and short tubes)
blocks.bestFor: Stop for a souvenir on the way to Bang Saen, an old-school dessert favourite, for those chasing Bib Gourmand finds on a light budget

blocks.name: Pathongko Mae Pranee
blocks.descHtml:
Pathongko Mae Pranee is a roadside cart selling takeaway only, with no seating, beside the Super Cheap Naka branch on Wirat Hongyok Road, Wichit sub-district, right next to Naka Market's tailgate flea market — the Super Cheap Naka coordinates are the easiest way to find it. Open Monday to Saturday, roughly half past five to ten in the morning, or until it sells out; closed Sundays. Prices are very easy on the wallet: four pieces of plain pathongko run about 10 baht, while filled versions like sausage or cheese run 10-20 baht a piece (prices from a 2021 interview, may have crept up a little since). Budget under 100 baht a person, easily.

No bookings needed and none are taken — just walk up and buy at the cart. There's a phone number, 087-386-8894, for questions, and cash only is accepted, so bring small notes to keep things moving. The best time to go is before 9am, since items often sell out before the listed closing time, especially on Saturdays when Naka Market draws a crowd. If you want every filling available, including crab and cheese, the earlier the better. It's just a few minutes' drive from Phuket Town, near the turn into the Naka area — park near the market and walk over. Read the full review →
blocks.signature: Dense, freshly fried pathongko with sausage, cheese, and crab fillings created by the second-generation owner
blocks.bestFor: A budget breakfast · for street-food fans · a stop before walking Naka Market
blocks.libCredit: Photo: Pathongko Mae Pranee official Facebook page

blocks.name: Roti Pa Day
blocks.descHtml:
Roti Pa Day sells from a roadside cart in front of Wat Mahawan on Tha Phae Road, on the eastern side of Chiang Mai's old town, a few minutes' walk from Tha Phae Gate. Prices start at 15 THB a piece (egg roti), 35 THB for the crispy roti, and 55 THB for the Nutella topping. It's open evenings until around midnight every day (roughly from 17:30–18:30 onward — as a roadside cart, the exact set-up time can shift from day to day). There's no booking system of any kind, cash only, and queue tickets are handed out at the cart.

During the cool season or on holiday nights, the queue of Chinese, Korean, and Japanese travelers runs long every evening. The trick is to arrive before 18:00 to grab a queue ticket as soon as the cart sets up, because only about 10 kilograms of dough — roughly 300 pieces — is made each day. Once it's gone, that's it, no more made. The easiest way to get there is to walk from the Tha Phae–Chang Moi area, or just tell a red-truck driver "Wat Mahawan, Tha Phae Road" — the whole city knows it. After buying, it's an easy walk on toward Tha Phae Gate or Warorot Market to keep exploring. Read the full review →
blocks.area: Tha Phae–Chang Moi (the old town's eastern gate)
blocks.signature: Crispy roti fried in coconut oil, egg-free dough, crisp outside and chewy inside
mustOrder: Plain crispy roti (35 THB) — egg-free dough fried in coconut oil, crisp outside and chewy inside
blocks.bestFor: MICHELIN-chasing street food fans capping off an evening in the old town — a light, walk-around dessert
blocks.zone: Tha Phae–Chang Moi (the old town's eastern gate)
blocks.libCredit: Photo: Thapae Rotee Padae official Facebook page

blocks.name: Sanpakoi Kanomjeen
blocks.descHtml:
Sanpakoi Kanomjeen is inside Talat Thong Kham (Gold Market) in the Sanpakoi area, on the east bank of the Ping River, near Khua Lek bridge and Tha Sadoi — just a few minutes across the bridge from the old city. Prices are easy on the wallet, 30–75 baht a plate, with a real meal for one person coming in under 100 baht. Open Monday to Saturday, 11:00–23:00, closed every Sunday — remember that closing day, since plenty of people have shown up to a locked door.

No advance booking needed — just walk in and sit down (walk-in only). There's a phone number, 061-301-8000, and LINE @sanpakoi for questions. It's busiest from lunch through dinner. If you want to sit comfortably without competing for a table, come in the late afternoon or evening, when the queue is noticeably lighter. And since the shop stays open until 11pm, dropping by for a late-night bite after a walk along the Ping riverside works out perfectly. The first dish to order is nam ngiao, followed by the shop's signature "nam lor," the mixed nam ngiao and nam ya recipe. Fresh vegetables are unlimited. Read the full review →
blocks.signature: Kanomjeen nam ngiao, and nam lor, the shop's signature mix of nam ngiao and nam ya
mustOrder: Kanomjeen nam lor (nam ngiao mixed with nam ya)
Kanomjeen coconut-milk nam ya / green curry chicken
blocks.bestFor: A budget meal with real local flavour, a favourite of northern Thai food fans, a late-night bite after the Ping riverside
blocks.libCredit: Photo: Sanpakoi Kanomjeen official Facebook page

blocks.name: Somsak Pu Ob (Charoen Rat)
blocks.descHtml:
Budget is roughly THB 150–300 per person, with a pot of baked crab or shrimp glass noodles starting around THB 220–300 and moving with seafood costs. Cash only, so bring bills — the stall doesn't take reservations through any channel, only a walk-in queue. The way to beat the line is to arrive before the stoves fire up at 15:30–16:00 and get your name down early. If you show up later, budget at least an hour of waiting.

The stall is open evenings only, roughly 16:00–21:30 Tuesday to Sunday, closed Monday — though published hours vary by source (some list 15:00–22:00), so a quick call to 081-400-0542 is the surest bet. Getting there is easy: take the BTS to Wongwian Yai and walk about 7 minutes to the mouth of Soi Charoen Rat 1 in Khlong San. One thing worth repeating: the branch with the Bib Gourmand is Charoen Rat 1 only — not the Lat Ya branch. Pin the right spot before you set off. Read the full review →
blocks.signature: Clay-pot crab baked with glass noodles, fresh off the charcoal stove curbside
mustOrder: Pu ob wun sen (crab baked with glass noodles)
Goong ob wun sen (shrimp baked with glass noodles)
blocks.bestFor: A dinner for a group of 3-4 friends craving Michelin-level clay-pot seafood at street-food prices, who don't mind queuing curbside

blocks.name: Tue Ka Ko Na Prince
blocks.descHtml:
Tue Ka Ko Na Prince is a roadside stall with no seating — takeaway only — located outside Prince Royal's College on Kaeo Nawarat Road, in the Wat Ket neighbourhood on the east bank of the Ping River, near Nawarat Bridge. Prices are very light: THB 20 a set, and eating your fill won't run past THB 100 per person. It's open roughly 09:00-16:00, but the key thing is it closes as soon as it sells out, not at a fixed time, and some sources say it's closed on Sundays — best to call ahead and check at 091-072-5891.

No booking needed and none is possible — just walk up and buy at the stall. They fry to order, one wok-load at a time, so the queue runs long right after school lets out. The best time to go is late morning to early afternoon, while stock is still full and before it gets crowded with parents picking up their kids. Order the tue ka ko with the three-flavour peanut dipping sauce, and add a bag of fried tofu — eat it hot for maximum crispness. If you're driving, look for parking around Kaeo Nawarat Road or the Wat Ket side, then walk to the school gate. Easy to combine with a wander around Wat Ket or a walk across the bridge to Warorot Market in the same trip. Read the full review →
blocks.signature: Tue Ka Ko — batter-dipped taro fried in three temperature-staged woks, light and crisp, never greasy, with a three-flavour peanut dipping sauce
mustOrder: Tue Ka Ko (crispy fried taro) with three-flavour peanut dipping sauce
blocks.bestFor: Street-food fans who want Bib Gourmand-level fried snacks for pocket change · a quick stop while wandering Wat Ket and Warorot Market
blocks.hours: Roughly 09:00-16:00, closes early once sold out
blocks.libCredit: Photo: Tue Ka Ko Na Prince official Facebook page

blocks.name: Leng Yentafo
blocks.descHtml:
Leng Yentafo sits on Thanon Klang Mueang, right in the center of Khon Kaen — easy to spot next to the 7-Eleven in front of Villa. Open daily 07:30–24:00 (some older sources list 07:00–03:00, so it's worth allowing some flexibility if you're heading there very late). Prices are easy on the wallet, under 100 THB a bowl. No reservation needed — just walk in and take a seat. Call 086-580-1259 if you have questions. One important thing to know: the shop accepts cash only, so bring small bills.

The best time to go is breakfast through lunch — MICHELIN named it one of the Best Breakfast Spots in Isan, and the queue is clearly shorter in the morning and midday than in the evening. The must-order dishes are the original-recipe yentafo, tom yum yentafo, house-made fish dumplings with fish balls, and deep-fried taro as a side. If the main branch is packed, there's a second branch near the Khon Kaen Hospital intersection as a backup option. Read the full review →

blocks.signature: Pink Yaowarat-style yentafo broth over 40 years old, served with house-made fish dumplings and fresh fish-and-shrimp balls made daily
mustOrder: House-made fish dumplings and fish balls
blocks.bestFor: A local breakfast-and-lunch spot for MICHELIN-followers on a budget under 100 THB, and for families craving Khon Kaen's legendary noodle soup

faq.q: Which street food spot should I try first?
faq.a: If you pick just one, make it K. Panich in Bangkok. Its mango sticky rice comes from a recipe passed down from the royal kitchens of Rama V and VI, sweetened with Chumphon coconut and Chiang Rai khao niao khiao ngu rice. One bite and you understand why Michelin singled it out.

A Pong Mae Sunee in Phuket, at 5 to 6 baht a piece, is an old-style coconut crepe grilled one at a time over charcoal, crisp at the edge and soft in the middle. Chiang Mai's Lung Khajohn Wat Ket also sells pork-filled sago dumplings at 20 baht for a box of seven.

faq.q: What is the must-try dish here?
faq.a: Somsak Pu Ob on Charoen Rat serves clay-pot crab and glass noodles baked over charcoal right on the street, and Jok Guay Jab in Khon Kaen does a Vietnamese-style pork rib noodle with pork sausage and a soft egg. Both were flagged by Michelin's inspectors.

faq.q: Where are these street food spots located?
faq.a: Chiang Mai has the most with four, followed by Bangkok and Khon Kaen with three each, Phuket with two, plus one apiece in Nakhon Ratchasima and Chon Buri. Chiang Mai alone covers Khao Soi Mae Sai, from 55 baht a bowl, and the nam ngiao rice noodles at Sanpakoi Kanomjeen.

faq.q: Are there any noodle or yentafo spots?
faq.a: Yes. Leng Yentafo in Khon Kaen pours a pink Yaowarat-style broth from a recipe over 40 years old, served with fish wontons and fish-and-shrimp balls made fresh daily. It is one of the noodle-focused entries that made the Bib Gourmand list.
